M&G Real Estate buys Melbourne build-to-rent property for A$215 million
article:
M&G Real Estate, a unit of global savings and investment company M&G, has purchased Bowen Crescent, a new completed build-to-rent (BTR) development in Melbourne, Australia, for A$215 million ($194 million).

The deal marks real estate investment manager’s foray into the Australian BTR sector, bringing assets under its Asia Living Property strategy to around US$500 million ($640 million). The portfolio now spans multi-family housing, purpose-built student accommodation, land lease communities and senior living.

Located close to the Melbourne CBD, the 17-storey Bowen Crescent has 215 one-, two- and three-bedroom rental apartments. There are also co-working facilities, a gym, a swimming pool, sauna and cold plunge.

It is a 150m away from Anzac Station, offering convenient access to the business district, major employment centres, and higher education hubs.

The acquisition builds on M&G Real Estate’s existing strategic partnership with Australian developer and asset manager Novus to develop purpose-built rental housing in Australia.

Demand for professional managed rental housing in Australia continues to grow, supported by strong demographic trends, said Jing Dong Lai, CEO of chief investment officer of M&G Real Estate Asia.

title: Fewer luxury non-landed residential deals as China's tax crackdown dampens sentiment: Huttons
article:
Singapore’s luxury non-landed housing market saw more muted activity in 3Q2026, as uncertainty brought on by China’s campaign to tax offshore wealth weighed on buyer sentiment.

In July, Chinese authorities announced a new 20% income tax on dividends and interest gained from offshore trusts, with a 90-day transition period for voluntary disclosure and settlemetntthat ended on Oct 22.

With the new rules, transferring a property into an offshore trust or income derived from an offshore trust "will be treated as income under the individual income tax law and will be taxable”, explained Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia.

The new regulations have prompted uncertainty in the past weeks as China’s wealthy sought clarifications on potential tax liabilities. Amid this stir, Singapore’s luxury condo market saw fewer transactions, according to Huttons.

Transaction volume of luxury non-landed homes

Luxury non-landed residential transactions totalled 66 deals in 3Q2026, declining 16.5% from 79 the previous quarter and falling 18.5% from 81 deals a year ago, based on data compiled in Huttons’ third quarter Prestige Report.

Huttons defines luxury non-landed homes as private residential units in the Core Central Region (CCR) with a strata area of 2,000 sq ft and above that transact for at least $5 million.

Luxury condo units sold in 3Q2026 had a total sales value of $509.6 million – a 24.3% decline from $673.4 million in 2Q2026 and 31.2% lower y-o-y.

Number of ultra-luxury non-landed homes ($10 million and above) transacted

Ultra-luxury non-landed units — CCR units sized 3,000 sq ft and above that transacted for at least $10 million — saw deals tumble to 11 units during the third quarter, compared to about 24 transactions the quarter before. The figure is the lowest since 4Q2025.

A 3,272 sq ft unit at Sculptura Ardmore that sold for $20 million ($6,112 psf) in September was the most expensive luxury condo deal in the third quarter. The unit at the 36-unit freehold development at Ardmore Park was purchased by an American foreigner.

On the other hand, leasing momentum rose in the luxury non-landed segment, which Huttons attributes to ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs) seeking safe havens like Singapore.

Rental volume rose by 11.2% q-o-q to 727 units in the third quarter, based on Huttons’ basket of luxury non-landed projects. The stronger demand bolstered rents, which increased 7.2% q-o-q.

Top 10 non-landed ultra-luxury homes sold in 3Q2026 by quantum

Seven GCB deals in 3Q2026

In the Good Class Bungalow (GCB) market, an estimated seven deals were recorded in 3Q2026, compared to eight the previous quarter.

This brings GCB deals to 24 for the first nine months of the year, two short of the 26 deals across the same period in 2025. In terms of sales value, the GCBs sold in the first three quarters fetched $880.2 million, 5% lower $927.2 million for the first nine months of 2025.

Top deals in GCB areas in 3Q2026 by price

Leasing activity also picked up in the GCB market, with rental volume jumping 50.6% q-o-q to an estimated 86 transactions. They included a GCB at Tanglin Hill leased for $108,888 per month – the first six-digit monthly rent recorded since 3Q2024, according to Huttons.

In the coming months, UHNWI buying sentiment will likely stay muted amid ongoing uncertainty from the tax crackdown, said Huttons CEO Yip.

“However, selective activity is being sustained by ongoing court-ordered state auctions of luxury apartments tied to the $3 billion money laundering investigation, which continue to draw opportunistic interest,” he added.

In any case, Singapore’s underlying market fundamentals remain resilient. “The strong pre-launch response for rare large-format units in The Park Residence (a 43-unit ultra-luxury project debuting in 4Q2026), paired with attractive entry opportunities from state-led auctions, underscores enduring long-term confidence in the nation's premier residential real estate,” Yip said.

title: ‘Supply onslaught’ to weigh on HDB resale market in 2027, but cash-rich buyers to support prices
article:
Despite an influx of supply, the HDB resale market could see modest price growth next year, supported by the “return of cash-rich buyers”, according to research by Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group.

In a 2027 outlook report on the HDB market published on Oct 26, the firm noted that resale flats will see an “onslaught of supply” next year and beyond, as more flats reach their minimum occupation period (MOP).

At the same time, recent policy changes could prompt more private homeowners to return to the HDB resale market.

In August, the government removed the 15-month waiting period for private housing owners looking to buy a non-subsidised HDB resale unit. This is expected to lead to more resale flat transactions, particularly for five-room, jumbo and executive resale flats.

“Cash-rich buyers will likely buy larger resale flats, as they are accustomed to spacious homes,” said Christine Sun, Realion’s chief researcher and strategist.

In addition, legislation lowering the consent threshold for collective sales of older developments was passed in September, potentially spurring en bloc activity. That would “unlock windfall gains for many private homeowners” that could fuel more big flat and million-dollar transactions, Sun added.

The opposing supply and demand factors will likely result in modest growth in resale flat prices next year, on the back of steady transaction volumes.

Realion estimates resale flat prices could grow between 2% and 4% in 2027, more than the 0% to 1% growth it is projecting for the whole of 2026. Resale flat volume in 2027 is expected to come in between 26,000 and 28,000 transactions, on par with its projection for this year.

Projected HDB resale volume and price trends for 2027

More MOP and BTO flats

Around 18,900 flats are expected to reach their MOP in 2027, nearly 5,500 more than the roughly 13,400 flats this year.

In addition, Realion projects almost 100,000 flats to reach their MOP between 2026 and 2030, and around 180,000 flats within the 10-year period from 2021 to 2030. The latter represents a 50% surge over the 120,000 flats that reached their MOP in the preceding decade.

The Build-to-Order (BTO) and Sale of Balance Flats (SBF) pipeline is also anticipated to remain robust, with around 22,000 to 26,000 BTO and SBF units projected to launch next year.

The pipeline, coupled with the recent increase in the income ceiling for BTO flats, could divert potential resale flat buyers to the primary market, where flats are generally cheaper.

In August, the monthly household income ceiling for eligible families buying BTO flats was raised from $14,000 to $16,000. “After the policy changes, we anticipate more buyers purchasing BTO flats instead of resale flats,” said Sun.

Two-speed market to intensify

Given the anticipated rise in demand from cash-rich buyers and the incoming supply of flats reaching their MOP, Sun believes the resale price gap between mature and non-mature estates could widen in 2027, intensifying a “two-speed” HDB resale market.

Median resale flat prices in mature estates rose by 9.6% in 2024 and 8.1% in 2025, outpacing the 6.4% and 5.2% gains recorded in non-mature estates for the same years. “This marked a reversal from 2022 and 2023, when non-mature estates recorded stronger price growth,” said Sun.

Looking ahead, she expects the price gap to expand. With cash-rich buyers “paying top dollar” for premium flats in established neighbourhoods, prices in mature estates are expected to see further growth, supported by more million-dollar transactions.

On the other hand, non-mature estates will likely see smaller and older flats come under pressure as supply increases, escalating competition among sellers. As such, resale prices there could stagnate, with some locations potentially seeing price corrections.

Slowing market

Realion’s outlook for 2027 comes amid a slower year for the HDB resale market. “Buying activities slowed noticeably in 2026, as sellers faced intense competition from a steady stream of BTO flats and a supply onslaught of resale flats reaching their MOP,” said Sun.

Nearly 13,500 flats are expected to have reached their MOP by the end of 2026, almost double the 6,973 flats last year.

New BTO supply has also remained consistent. Including the year's last BTO exercise coming up in November, Realion estimates 19,614 units will have launched this year, compared to 19,723 units last year.

Amid the surge in resale flat supply and competition from the BTO market, the HDB Resale Price Index posted its first quarterly decline in nearly seven years at the start of the year, falling 0.1% q-o-q in 1Q2026.

It eased further in the subsequent quarters, declining 0.3% and 0.1% in the second and third quarters, respectively.

However, premium resale flat deals continued to climb, with 4,607 flats sold for at least $800,000 in the first nine months of the year. They included 1,497 homes that fetched at least $1 million and 12 units sold for $1.6 million or more.

title: How Chinese home-tech brands are making Singapore homes smarter
article:
Singaporeans are no strangers to paying for convenience. In a city where work, family and everyday responsibilities compete for time, we have long looked for ways to make daily life a little easier, whether that means having dinner delivered after a long day at work or groceries arriving at the doorstep.

Increasingly, that same expectation is shaping the home.

We are seeing technology move beyond helping people complete household tasks towards taking more of those tasks off their hands altogether.

For example, robot vacuums no longer just clean floors. More advanced models can map the home, navigate around obstacles, empty their own dustbins and double up as mops that can even wash themselves.

Connected-home technology can automate everything from lighting and curtains to security, reducing the number of small interactions homeowners need to think about each day.

A new generation of Chinese home-tech brands is finding a place in Singapore homes, signalling changing consumer expectations of the technology they live with.

From more features to less effort

For homeowners, the appeal of automation is not necessarily the technology itself. It is what that technology can give back.

Take cleaning as an example. Brands such as Ecovacs have steadily expanded what a robot vacuum can take care of independently, with advanced models offering functions such as intelligent home mapping, automatic dustbin emptying and self-cleaning mopping.

On Lazada, we have seen shoppers increasingly gravitate towards premium, self-maintaining robot vacuums.

Flagship products in this tier have gained a disproportionate share of demand within the robot vacuum category, suggesting that consumers are not only embracing automated cleaning, but are increasingly investing in products that can take more of the work off their hands.

The same desire for simplicity is appearing elsewhere in the home.

Aqara, for instance, offers connected products spanning lighting, curtains, sensors and security that can work together around household routines. Instead of managing each device individually, homeowners can set up routines that take care of small actions automatically.

Individually, these are hardly the biggest demands on our day, but anyone who has come home after a long day to floors that still need cleaning, rushed out wondering whether the lights were switched off or questioned halfway to work whether they locked the door knows how quickly the small things add up. They do not just take time. They take up headspace too.

That is where we see the definition of convenience evolving. The question is becoming less about "What can this device do?" and more about "What will I no longer need to do?"

Winning a place in the home takes more than technology

With more brands and products to choose from, getting consumers to consider something new is not simply a matter of offering more features.

Singapore shoppers have no shortage of choice. While brand recognition matters, particularly for higher-value purchases, consumers today are doing their homework before deciding what deserves a place in their homes.

Our 2026 eCommerce Savvy Shopper Report: Southeast Asia , developed jointly by Lazada and Cube, found that nine in 10 Southeast Asian shoppers frequently check product reviews and ratings, while seven in 10 research products beyond the platform.

This gives brands an opportunity to be considered for what their products can offer, rather than on familiarity alone.

We are seeing this play out among Chinese home-tech brands such as Ecovacs and Aqara, which have developed increasingly sophisticated products spanning automation, connectivity and functionality at different price points.

Ecovacs today ranks among the top three robot vacuum brands on Lazada Singapore, with its self-emptying and self-mopping flagship models among the most searched in the category.

Aqara has carved out a similarly strong position in the connected-home space, growing its footprint across lighting, curtains, sensors and security.

The increasing popularity of such products points to growing interest in what these brands have to offer.

However, there is a danger in equating a smarter home with simply having more technology.

For most homeowners, the goal is not to build the most technologically advanced home possible. It is to make everyday life easier.

A good place to start is therefore not with the product, but with the problem.

What is the repetitive task or small frustration you would most like to remove from your day? From there, consider how much attention the technology will still require after it is set up, whether it pairs with devices already in your home and whether you will actually make full use of the additional features you are paying for.

After all, a feature only creates value if it makes life meaningfully easier.

Making smarter choices in a crowded market

As home technology becomes more sophisticated, choosing the right product can also become more complicated.

A robot vacuum, smart lock or connected lighting system can represent a significant investment, and homeowners must weigh price, features, compatibility and whether a product will genuinely make everyday life easier.

E-commerce has made that comparison easier. On Lazada, for example, shoppers can compare brands, specifications and reviews, and purchase through official brand stores on LazMall.

During our recent 9.9 Mega Brands Sale in Singapore, more than three in four orders came through LazMall, reflecting the importance of trusted channels.

For homeowners, smarter choices go beyond prices and specifications. Check official brand stores, read ratings and reviews, and look into warranties, returns and after-sales support, particularly for higher-value purchases. These provide a fuller picture of ownership long after delivery.

Brands such as Ecovacs and Aqara show how expectations are changing across automated cleaning, lighting and security.

But the smartest product is not necessarily the one with the longest list of features. It is the one that fits naturally into the realities of your life and seamlessly takes a task off your plate.

Because for a busy household, sometimes the most valuable thing technology can give us is not another feature. It is one less thing to think about.

title: Why Smart Investors Buy Small-Cap Stocks (And Why Big Funds Can’t)
article:
Small-cap stocks
– companies with a market capitalisation below S$1 billion, often sitting around S$400 million to S$500 million – might look like peanuts next to giant Singapore blue-chip banks.
Yet, these smaller companies represent some of the most compelling opportunities in the market.
Because fewer people follow them, they often sit as hidden gems right under our noses.
The Big Fund Dilemma
Why don’t managers of multi-billion-dollar funds scoop up these bargain small-caps?
Imagine you are hosting a dinner party for a thousand guests.
You can only choose restaurants massive enough to seat a thousand people.
There might be a fantastic little restaurant around the corner charging a fraction of the price with food just as good as a five-star hotel’s, but you simply cannot go there with a thousand people.
Fund managers face the exact same structural limitation.
They manage billions of dollars.
Even if a fund manager bought an entire S$200 million company outright, it wouldn’t move the needle for their total portfolio.
As retail investors putting S$10,000, S$20,000 or S$30,000 into the market, we don’t have that handicap.
We can comfortably hold
blue chips
and real estate investment trusts (REITs) while taking full advantage of the neglected smaller companies big funds are forced to ignore.
Simple Businesses Beat Opaque Financials
Analysing a small-cap is no different from evaluating a large-cap: you are buying a piece of a business.
In fact, small-caps are often much easier to understand.
Major financial institutions can act like complex sausage machines – money goes in, something complicated happens inside, and profit comes out the other end.
Their annual reports run to hundreds of pages, and what happens behind closed doors can be opaque even to seasoned analysts.
Compare that to a small consumer business selling everyday snacks like curry puffs.
Aside from the secret recipe, there is no mystery inside the business model, and the financial statements are straightforward to digest.
The Misconception About Size and Risk
Many investors assume large companies are inherently safe and small companies are inherently dangerous, but size alone is no shield against distress.
A massive property developer carrying billions in debt can go under during a downturn, whereas a cash-generative small-cap sitting on a net-cash balance sheet cannot easily go bust.
Furthermore, heavy analyst coverage does not make a large-cap stock safe, as analysts often herd together to avoid standing out from the crowd.
Finally, while trying to call the CEO of a major bank for a quick chat will get you nowhere, management at a small-cap is far more accessible to interested shareholders wanting to understand the operations.
Market volatility affects all share prices, but fundamental business risk diminishes the better you understand what you own.
Get Smart: Conviction Beats Market Volatility
Small-cap investing gives retail investors a distinct structural edge over institutional players.
By focusing on simple,
cash-generative businesses
with strong balance sheets, you can spot value long before the rest of the market catches on.

title: Memory stocks lost their shine despite strong earnings
article:
(Oct 27): Sandisk Corp, Micron Technology Inc, Seagate Technology Holdings plc and Western Digital Corp were among the stock market’s biggest winners in the first six months of the year as demand from the artificial intelligence (AI) build out seemed insatiable.

But since then momentum has turned against the shares of AI component manufacturers, like the makers of semiconductors, memory and storage, with investors questioning the durability of massive spending commitments. As a result, Sandisk, Micron, Seagate and Western Digital are in the bottom 10% of the S&P 500 Index in the second half of 2026, and even blowout earnings haven’t been enough to reverse the trend.

“The market is telling you that expectations are changing for how long the earnings boom is going to last for these companies,” said Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments.

This dynamic was apparent last week, when Western Digital’s results and forecast late on Thursday blew past expectations and the company boosted its dividend, but the shares fell 3% on Friday because of concerns that AI spending had peaked. At the end of September, Micron beat projections for profits and revenue and gave an outlook that was far better than expected, but the stock is down 15% since then.

Seagate is the next up, with its earnings due after the close on Tuesday, and analysts expect the company’s net income to triple. Sandisk follows on Thursday, and its earnings per share are projected to soar more than 6,100%.

See also: Applied Materials ups stake in BE Semiconductor to about 20%

“Now that the trade has gotten long in the tooth, what can turn it around?” said Andre Bakhos, president of Ingenium Analytics. “Not only will you need great earnings, but you’ll need to see follow-through next quarter and the one after that.”

This growth is being fuelled by massive spending on AI, which isn’t seen slowing anytime soon. Last week, Meta Platforms Inc boosted its capital expenditure plans for the year. Wall Street anticipates that Microsoft Corp, Amazon.com Inc and Alphabet Inc will affirm or raise their AI spending plans when they report earnings this week. And on Monday, Anthropic PBC filed for its long-awaited initial public offering, which is expected to demonstrate the enduring strength of the AI trade, sending memory and storage stocks higher.

The problem is investors are becoming increasingly skeptical about the payoff from all this AI spending, particularly now that so much of it is being financed by debt. For example, a gauge of Meta’s credit risk hit a fresh record after the company revealed its projected capital expenditures. Add in a challenging economic backdrop featuring high oil prices and interest rates, and it’s easy to see where the pessimism is coming from.

See also: Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo draws early complaints of the screen cracking

This helps explain why the once high-flying memory and storage stocks have had their wings clipped. Since the start of the third quarter, Sandisk and Western Digital are down more than 44%, while Seagate has lost 33% and Micron has sunk 22%. While that’s taken a chunk out of their year-to-date gains, all remain up significantly in 2026, led by Sandisk’s almost 430% surge, which is the second-best performance in the S&P 500.

“There used to be this concentrated FOMO mentality surrounding memory, but now investors are starting to weigh the risk of all that expenditure and debate whether it can keep going,” Bakhos said.

In other words, the group needs external validation from the big AI spenders to keep the rally going. If they reassure investors that their plans are leading to profits, confidence in the group should rise because capital expenditures will remain elevated.

“The fundamental story seems largely intact over the near term, but risks are obvious and the bear case remains,” Tigay said. “Should they not live up to expectations, demand could fall off a cliff.”

Seagate and Sandisk are expected to see slowing growth in the coming years, according to analysts’ estimates. Seagate’s revenue is projected to rise about 56% in its 2027 fiscal year, which ends in June, before decelerating to 37% in fiscal 2028 and 20% in fiscal 2029. Sandisk’s revenue for its 2027 fiscal year, which also ends in June, is projected to leap 140%, but the pace is expected to slow to 20% in fiscal 2028, before actually declining 7% in fiscal 2029.

One positive for the group is the shares aren’t expensive. Micron trades at five times earnings estimated over the next 12 months, making it the second-cheapest stock in the S&P 500 after Charter Communications Inc, and Sandisk is close behind at less than six times. Meanwhile Western Digital’s multiple is around 12, and Seagate’s is 15. All are trading at a discount to the broader market, with the S&P 500 valued at roughly 19 times estimated earnings and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index at 20.

While some Wall Street pros caution that the historical cyclicality of memory demand makes those low multiples contrarian warning signals, the size and scale of the AI buildout could render comparisons to previous cycles irrelevant. Analysts’ price target for Seagate indicates the shares will rise more than 70% over the next 12 months, while Sandisk is expected to climb more than 80%. Of the 74 stocks in the S&P information technology sector, Micron, Seagate, Sandisk and Western Digital are among the top seven in return potential, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

“People rightfully get nervous when you see a selloff, because you don’t know if it’s the top or just some air coming out before another cycle higher,” Bakhos said. “Profit takers are winning the battle now, but I think the long-term holders are in a strong position.”

title: Singapore’s EMA backs grid resilience projects with $14.9 mil
article:
Singapore’s Energy Market Authority (EMA) has awarded $14.9 million to four projects aimed at keeping its electricity grid reliable as more solar panels and electric vehicle chargers connect to it.

The work comes as Singapore plans for higher power demand. In a five-year infrastructure plan announced yesterday, EMA says peak demand could rise from 8.6 gigawatts in August to as much as 13 gigawatts by 2031.

EMA awarded $8.7 million to two projects by SP PowerAssets under the SP Technology Laboratory, which EMA and SP Group established to develop ways to prepare the grid for future needs.

One project will use AI and data to guide maintenance and renewal decisions for grid infrastructure. The other will test ways to manage voltage and power quality as more solar panels and electric vehicle chargers connect to the grid.

Meanwhile, Yokogawa Engineering Asia received $4.2 million to develop support that can respond quickly when the power system is disturbed. Its project will examine whether batteries, solar inverters, industrial electricity users and EVs can be coordinated to provide that support.

The remaining $2 million went to Green Union. It will develop ways to coordinate solar panels, battery storage systems and EVs so they can contribute to grid operations and make better use of existing infrastructure. The project is funded under a joint grant by EMA and the Korean Institute of Energy Technology Evaluation and Planning (KETEP), which supports industry-led research into using such resources to strengthen the power system.

See also: Sembcorp and ST Engineering prepare for nuclear future

Separately, EMA has helped update guidance on how companies substantiate claims that they use renewable electricity in Singapore. Enterprise Singapore, through the Singapore Standards Council, revised Singapore Standard 673 with EMA and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry.

Under the revised standard, companies making such claims should use renewable energy certificates tied to electricity supplied to Singapore’s grid. This includes certificates from domestic renewable generation and approved electricity imports connected to the grid.

See also: Singapore shields itself from energy risks as Indonesia cuts gas

Companies can still buy certificates from overseas renewable projects that do not supply electricity to Singapore to support renewable energy development.

The standard says they should not use those certificates for market-based Scope 2 claims about electricity consumed here. Scope 2 covers emissions associated with electricity a company purchases.

title: Applied Materials ups stake in BE Semiconductor to about 20%
article:
(Oct 27): Applied Materials Inc boosted its stake in fellow chip-equipment maker BE Semiconductor Industries NV and said it plans to work more closely with the European company, which is becoming a more important part of the artificial intelligence (AI) computing supply chain.

Applied’s stake will increase to about 20% of outstanding shares, the US company said in a statement on Monday. The company first disclosed a 9% stake in BE Semiconductor, known as Besi, last year.

Besi shares rose as much as 10% in Amsterdam trading on Tuesday, the biggest intraday gain since March. The stock has gained 19% this year, giving it a market value of about €12.9 billion. Applied closed 2.7% higher at US$387.59 in New York on Monday.

Companies that make equipment for AI and the data centres that run the technology are seeing surging demand. Besi specialises in hybrid bonding, a technology used in chip assembly that boosts AI performance. Last week, the company rebuffed analysts’ concerns that larger chip-equipment maker ASML Holding NV was emerging as a competitor.

Applied’s investment follows a six-year collaboration between the two companies. Besi also recently joined Applied’s new chip-equipment research facility known as the EPIC Center.

Though Applied described its investment as “long term”, the company said a bigger takeover is not in the works. “Applied currently has no intention to increase its investment in Besi beyond approximately 20%, and Applied does not intend to seek board representation at Besi,” the company said.

See also: Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo draws early complaints of the screen cracking

title: Coca-Cola raises guidance, buoyed by soda sales abroad
article:
(Oct 27): Coca-Cola Co raised its 2026 full-year outlook on strong international demand for soda, especially its zero-sugar drinks.

The beverage company now sees organic sales increasing at least 5% this year, rather than growing about that much. Coca-Cola had already raised its guidance in July, pointing to the company’s increasing confidence in the year’s results.

“Our results this quarter demonstrate our system’s sustained momentum, giving us confidence in our updated full-year guidance,” CEO Henrique Braun said in a statement.

The Atlanta-based company said it saw 5% growth in unit case volume sales of sparkling soft drinks, including 16% growth of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar and 6% growth of Diet Coke. However, in North America, growth in Coca-Cola soda was offset by a decline in water, sports, coffee and tea. Sales volume in North America was flat, coming in below the average of analysts’ estimates of 2.3% growth.

Shares of Coca-Cola were little changed at 7.28am in premarket New York trading. The stock has gained almost 33% this year through Monday’s close, compared with a 12% increase in the S&P 500 Index. PepsiCo stock has declined 6% over the same period.

Coca-Cola’s third-quarter adjusted earnings per share were 91 cents, topping the average of analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg. Organic sales, which strip out items such as currency volatility, rose 7%, above expectations.

See also: Starbucks says it’s not buying Chipotle, dousing deal rumours

Coca-Cola’s widening portfolio of beverages is reaching more shoppers, with zero-sugar soda, higher-protein Fairlife milk and water as many consumers turn away from traditional full-calorie soft drinks. Coca-Cola has also nabbed some recent wins against rival PepsiCo Inc, including taking over KFC’s US restaurants.

title: ST Engineering won $5.6 bil worth of new contracts in 3QFY2026
article:
Singapore Technologies Engineering has won contracts worth some $5.6 billion in 3QFY2026, bringing the nine-month total to $13.2 billion.

The strong third quarter was driven by broad-base wins across all three business segments, with commercial aerospace securing $1.4 billion, defence & public security $1.8 billion and urban solutions & satcom $2.4 billion.

According to ST Engineering, contracts won by USS include those for major train works in Taiwan and also Singapore.

Its electronic road tolling business also won contracts to advance Dubai's tolling system, modernise tolling infrastructure for the Tampa-Hillsborough Expressway Authority, and deliver back-office solutions and RFID tags in the US as well.

Also, in Singapore, the company won contracts to provide integrated smart security management solutions for public and private sector customers.

The Satcom business secured various contracts for the deployments of its multi-orbit ‘Intuition’ platform including one with Datacom and expanded mission-critical government and defence networks. It also supported satellite operator modernisation programmes across Europe, Africa, the Middle East and Asia.

See also: Yangzijiang Maritime to sell six vessels for US$308 million

For the company's commercial aerospace segment, new contracts won include its first Airbus A220 airframe heavy maintenance contract with an Asia-Pacific operator, expanding its support capabilities for next-generation narrowbody platforms beyond the Airbus A320neo and Boeing 737 MAX.

It also secured airframe maintenance agreements with Asia Pacific airline customers, an exclusive two-year CFM56-7B engines Performance Restoration Shop Visit services agreement with Hebei Airlines and a multi-year component MRO agreement with Collins Aerospace.

As for its DPS segment, it won a five-year contract to supply 40mm ammunition to the UK Ministry of Defence, alongside additional ammunition orders from international customers.

See also: Soilbuild Construction wins $103 mil worth of new contracts

The digital systems under DPS also won projects for its data centre services, public safety digital infrastructure and defence command-and-control systems. A satellite ground station and maintenance programme was also secured in Sweden.

In cybersecurity, it secured contracts for new products, services and solutions from defence and commercial customers in Singapore.

Its Marine and Defence Aerospace businesses in Singapore expanded MRO support for the United States Naval Ship fleet and international C-130 operators.

ST Engineering shares closed at $10.16 on Oct 27, down 0.2%.

title: Universal Music discussed going private with buyout firms
article:
(Oct 27): Universal Music Group, the world’s largest record company, has discussed going private with a few prominent Wall Street firms, according to people familiar with the matter.

Universal’s management held preliminary conversations with private equity firms including Apollo Global Management Inc, TPG Inc and Blackstone Inc earlier this year, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the talks were confidential. The board of the company, with a market value of €29 billion (RM132.74 billion), is aware of the discussions, they added.

The conversations have not progressed nor has Universal, home to acts including Taylor Swift, The Weeknd and Kendrick Lamar, begun a sales process, the people said.

The company declined to comment, as did the private equity firms. Universal’s sagging share price has prompted many at the company and on Wall Street to wonder whether the music giant would be better off as a private firm.

Shares in Universal rose as much as 6% in Amsterdam trading on Tuesday, the biggest intraday gain since April. The stock has declined about 27% this year and trades below the price at which the company first went public in 2021. Catalogues and other music assets are trading at much higher multiples than Universal and rival Warner Music Group on the private market.

Universal, led by CEO Lucian Grainge, was already the target of one takeover attempt this year when shareholder Bill Ackman made an offer to buy the Amsterdam-listed company and move its listing to the US. Universal rejected the bid but the company’s largest shareholder agreed with Ackman that the firm is undervalued. Universal is the largest and most successful of the three major record label groups, the distributor of nine of the 10 best-selling acts in the world last year. Sony Group Corp is another major competitor.

See also: Orange boosts profit outlook after Africa, Middle East growth

“We think that the price is not right at all,” Cyrille Bollore, whose family owns a 30% stake in Universal Music Group, said at his firm’s shareholder meeting in May. Bollore praised Universal as one of his family’s best investments and a hedge against an economic downturn. “Perhaps we’ll sell a few per cent one day. We’ll see. But we can’t sell too early.”

Any deal would require the assent of the Bollore family, which owns more than 30% of the firm between the personal holdings of Vincent Bollore, Cyrille’s father, and Vivendi, their media company. Vivendi used to own Universal Music before the company was spun out as a separate public company.

The Bollores haven’t signalled interest in selling their full position. Nor has Chinese internet giant Tencent Holdings Ltd, which owns more than 11%. Taking Universal public was lucrative for the Bollores and a handful of senior leaders who had stock. The company has since struggled to satisfy investors.

See also: Japan vows to address cyber attack on FX with urgency

Record labels have surrendered market share to independent distributors offering more artist-friendly terms. The streaming market that boosted sales for the last decade has slowed in the US and Western Europe over the last couple of years. The fastest-growing markets are in Latin America and Asia, regions where the major record labels are less dominant.

The biggest drag on the stock of Universal and Warner Music has been anxiety about artificial intelligence. AI has produced a surge in the number of songs getting uploaded to streaming services, which analysts and investors fear will dilute the labels’ share of listening and earnings.

Grainge has said Universal isn’t at risk of dilution. “We anticipated the rise of AI slop and we anticipated the potential for fraud,” Grainge said on a call with analysts in July. “Music platforms should reward creativity and guard against illegally trained AI models pumping AI slop or fraud designed to divert royalties from artists, songwriters, labels and music publishers.”

Universal has expressed concern about AI companies violating its copyrights, as file-sharing websites did during the internet boom. Universal sued Suno, the largest AI music company, as well as Anthropic.

title: Aramco contains fire near Ras Tanura oil hub after attack — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 27): Saudi Arabia contained a fire near its biggest oil export terminal at Ras Tanura on the Persian Gulf following an attack in the region, a person with knowledge of the matter said.

The blaze occurred during the early hours of Tuesday near facilities operated by state producer Saudi Aramco, the person said, asking not to be identified because the matter is private. The extent of the damage wasn’t immediately clear.

The company’s press office and the kingdom’s Energy Ministry didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure has come under repeated attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militants in recent weeks, with Aramco’s headquarters, a major oil field and refineries in the kingdom’s western region targeted. Ras Tanura, located in the east, hosts crucial facilities for loading oil tankers, plus the kingdom’s biggest refinery and a swathe of storage tanks.

Saudi Arabia said on Tuesday that air defences intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region.

See also: Oil declines as Iran diplomacy picks up before Israeli, US votes

Oil reversed earlier losses, with Brent crude trading near US$116 a barrel in London. Prices have jumped about 13% so far this month as traders weigh the potential for a resumption of fighting between the US and Iran.

Both sides have held off major military operations in recent weeks, while Saudi Arabia has suffered attacks from Iran-backed groups like the Houthis in Yemen and militias in Iraq.

When the conflict began in February, Aramco began sending the bulk of its exports from its Red Sea coast after Iran blocked much of the traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. In recent weeks, the company has been stepping up crude exports from the Persian Gulf again.

See also: Woodside sells stake in long-stalled Timor-Leste LNG project

That’s partly because tanker operators have been finding ways to restore shipping flows through Hormuz, with traffic reaching almost prewar levels. It also reflects growing Houthi threats to shipping and ports in the Red Sea.

title: CGAC, SGX RegCo’s proposed changes to corporate governance code and listing rules include cap on directorships
article:
The Corporate Governance Advisory Committee (CGAC) and the Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) are proposing several changes to the Code of Corporate Governance (Code) and SGX Listing Rules. The changes are meant to complement with the Equities Market Review Group’s earlier announced initiatives while helping to strengthen corporate governance and sustain investor confidence, says CGAC and SGX RegCo in a statement on Oct 27.

CGAC and SGX RegCo have launched a public consultation to obtain feedback on the proposed changes. The consultation will run from Oct 27, 2026 to Jan 27, 2027. CGAC and SGX RegCo’s proposed changes fall under three broad areas: facilitating effective implementation of the Code, enhancing board independence and quality as well as sharpening the focus on value creation.

“We are not trying to create rigid, restrictive rules about what companies disclose and how they disclose it. We are trying to create a structure and framework that helps every enterprise reach its growth objectives,” SGX RegCo CEO Tan Boon Gin says of the proposed changes.

Under the first area, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing that the Code and Practice Guidance be updated to reflect intended outcomes and illustrative examples. This will help to provide greater clarity on how the Code’s principles can be achieved.

Code provisions apply to listed companies on a comply-or-explain basis while the provisions under the Practice Guidance are purely voluntary. Compliance with SGX Listing Rules is mandatory for all listed companies.

The changes under the second area aim to make boards more effective by ensuring strong governance arrangements and the appointment of high-quality directors. To that end, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing a new Code provision for companies where the CEO is concurrently serving as the board chair to explain how the chair’s role is effectively fulfilled and to disclose the safeguards in place. Companies will be required under the SGX Listing Rules to appoint a lead independent director when the chair is not independent.

See also: Seven Singapore-listed names among ‘global sector leaders’ in annual real estate ESG benchmark

Other proposed changes to the SGX Listing Rules include requiring key board committees, including the nominating committee, remuneration committee and audit committee to be chaired by an independent director and comprise a majority of independent directors.

Companies will also be required to disclose, explicitly, the selection criteria and considerations for board appointments as well as whether board members have undergone professional development activities relevant to their roles. In addition, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing a cap on the number to listed-entity directorships an individual can hold at any time to no more than five.

As for the third and final area, CGAC and SGX RegCo are proposing refinements to Code provisions to reinforce the responsibility of boards to oversee strategy, long-term value creation and investor engagement. Additionally, companies will be required to disclose their capital management policies.

See also: SIAS CEO welcomes rising corporate governance standards but notes gap between large and small companies

Earlier, on Sept 23, SGX RegCo introduced new rules requiring companies to disclose their dividend policy to shareholders. The changes, which apply to annual reports for financial years commencing on or after Jan 1, 2027, do not require issuers to commit to a dividend payout.

“A boilerplate disclosure is better than no disclosure at all,” Tan says. “In a disclosure-based regime, a baseline disclosure forms an essential starting point for investor assessment and engagement. It gives the market a benchmark. Investors can compare issuers: The one with a detailed capital management policy will naturally capture more trust and a premium. The one with a boilerplate will be left behind.”

CGAC says it will consider the feedback received before making its final recommendations to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and SGX on the Code and SGX Listing Rules respectively. Thereafter, MAS and SGX will consider CGAC’s recommendations before deciding on the final amendments, implementation timelines and transitional arrangements.

title: Pop Mart's 3Q sales fall up to 50% as Labubu fad cools
article:
(Oct 27): Pop Mart International Group Ltd reported a decline in third-quarter (3Q) sales from a year earlier, hurt by fading Labubu momentum and a tough base of comparison following last year’s blockbuster results.

Overall revenue fell as much as 50% from a year ago in the three months ended September, according to Pop Mart’s latest business update based on preliminary data. That compares with revenue growth of about 250% in the year-ago period. Revenue in China declined 25% to 30%, while sales from the Americas fell 70% to 75%.

The downturn underscores the volatility that can accompany an unexpected viral hit. Demand for Labubu — the snaggle-toothed monster plush — reached fever pitch in 2025 with everyone from K-pop idols to Hollywood celebrities and ordinary consumers seeking one. The results also highlight mounting pressure on the company as investors grapple with softening demand this year in its home market alongside persistent weakness across overseas operations.

While Pop Mart has described 2026 as “a year of adjustment”, investors are concerned that the slowdown could extend into 2027. HSBC Holdings plc cut its revenue forecasts for 2027 and 2028 by 8% and 9%, respectively, in a research note released ahead of the results, citing expectations for “a longer road to stabilisation”. The bank also lowered its 2026 sales estimate to 33.2 billion yuan from 34.6 billion yuan previously.

In a bid to maximise brand exposure and keep consumer buzz alive, Pop Mart continued expanding its retail footprint through flagship locations in key domestic and international markets. The company opened a three-story flagship store near West Lake in Hangzhou and launched its European flagship on Boulevard Haussmann in Paris in September. It also rolled out new releases tied to popular intellectual properties, including Twinkle Twinkle and Dimoo, during 3Q.

title: French consumer confidence drops to 13-year low following riots
article:
(Oct 27): French consumer confidence plummeted to its lowest level in 13 years in October as households reckoned with multiple shocks from a bond market selloff to protests that descended into rioting.

The monthly gauge dropped five points to 80 with respondents becoming more concerned about their financial situation, living standards and unemployment, statistics agency Insee said on Tuesday. That’s below the median estimate of 85 in a Bloomberg survey and lower than any economist forecast.

 

The reading has been stuck below its long-term average of 100 for five years amid bouts of inflation and political and budget instability.

But the backdrop has worsened significantly in recent weeks with the minority government entering another showdown over austerity measures, a surge in borrowing costs as investors dump French bonds and an escalation of student protests.

The tensions boiled over on Oct 17 with violence breaking out around cost-of-living demonstrations, looting across the country and thousands of arrests.

Insee’s latest consumer confidence measure doesn’t reflect the full impact of the upheaval: while the the cutoff was Oct 19, most of the responses are collected at the start of the three-week survey period.

See also: Germany’s business outlook in October unexpectedly improves for sixth month

“Weak sentiment is likely to weigh on spending as political uncertainty increases. This brings further downside risks to our fourth-quarter growth forecast,” says Jean Dalbard, economist at Bloomberg Economics.

In an attempt to calm the unrest that began with students blocking high schools, the French government announced on Monday it will overhaul the system for allocating university places, limit some class sizes and provide loans for building renovations.

See also: EU plans to hit China with more import curbs in early 2027 — Bloomberg

But protests are set to continue on Saturdays as well as a day of demonstrations and strikes on Nov 5 that’s backed by the country’s biggest trade unions.

President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday he would also maintain a heightened security presence, similar to the deployment that ensured relative calm on Saturday.

“It’s not normal that six months before a presidential election, our country should be in such a state of turmoil,” he said after visiting police in Marseille. “Some people are happy to see disorder, I’m not — never again another Oct 17.”

Details of Insee’s survey showed that assessments of past living standards dropped to the lowest since the agency began measuring in 1972. Meanwhile, unemployment expectations rose to the highest since the Covid pandemic and consumers’ outlook for their financial situation was the gloomiest in four years.

The report also showed heightened inflation expectations as the proportion of households who foresee price increases in the next twelve months advanced.

Data on Friday is expected to show inflation accelerated further to 3.6% this month. A reading of gross domestic product, also due that day, will likely reveal that the economy expanded only 0.1% in the third quarter after stagnating in the previous three months and contracting at the start of the year.
